name: Real estate, housing and construction
summary: Construction is Ethiopia's largest industrial activity: the National Bank of Ethiopia reports it contributed around 23 percent of GDP and grew 9.0 percent in 2023/24. Urban population is growing by about 4.6 percent a year, and the World Bank estimates the country needs nearly 400,000 new housing units a year. The government has opened residential ownership to foreign nationals, signed affordable-housing PPPs, and is tendering more mixed-use housing PPP sites in Addis Ababa.

indicators.label: Construction sector contribution to GDP
indicators.value: around 23 percent of GDP (70.1 percent of the industrial sector in the text; Table 1.2 shows 72.1 percent)

indicators.label: New urban housing units needed
indicators.value: nearly 400,000 new housing units per year to meet new demand (annual projected demand of 381,000 plus replacement housing)

indicators.label: Government housing supply versus demand
indicators.value: meeting only 10% of annual demand; 60% of households in large cities live in rental units

indicators.label: Homes built and under construction (government statement)
indicators.value: around one million homes built over the past five years; over 265,000 more under construction

indicators.label: Lemi National Cement Factory capacity
indicators.value: 150,000 quintals per day; produces 50 percent of the cement made by factories across the country

returnsNote: No international institution or Ethiopian government source we reviewed publishes an average return on investment for this sector. The closest published indicators included are Treasury bill yields (9.74 percent in 2023/24; 14.4 percent on new issuances in April 2026) and the economy-wide bank lending rate (average 14.25 percent, range 7.00 to 21.50 percent, in 2023/24).

opportunities.title: Affordable housing PPPs in Addis Ababa
opportunities.detail: The Ministry of Finance invited expressions of interest to design, finance, build, operate, maintain and transfer four affordable housing PPP projects covering eight mixed-use commercial and residential sites in four clusters in Addis Ababa (responses due June 1, 2026).

opportunities.title: Signed housing PPPs
opportunities.detail: Seven private developers signed PPP agreements with the Ministry of Finance on July 3, 2025, four of them for affordable housing, under PPP Proclamation No. 1076/2018.

opportunities.title: Residential property open to foreign buyers
opportunities.detail: The House of Peoples' Representatives passed a proclamation on July 1, 2025 that allows foreign nationals to own residential real estate in Ethiopia, subject to the procedures in the new law.

opportunities.title: Corridor development pipeline
opportunities.detail: The second phase of Addis Ababa's corridor development delivered 135 km of roads, 246 km of pedestrian walkways, 141 km of bicycle lanes and 53 bridges (reported to the City Council in July 2025).

opportunities.title: Expressway PPPs
opportunities.detail: The Ministry of Finance lists three expressway projects (Adama-Awash, Awash-Mieso, Mieso-Dire Dawa), about 357 km with an approximate cost of USD 871 million, among its PPP programs.

opportunities.title: Housing finance build-out
opportunities.detail: A framework agreement between the National Bank of Ethiopia and IFC, witnessed by the Prime Minister in September 2026, aims to support the construction of 1.5 million affordable homes.

incentives.detail: Exemption from duties and other taxes on imports of machinery, equipment and construction material (Ethiopian Investment Commission incentive list).
Up to 15 years income-tax holiday for industrial park developers, and a 60 to 80 year charge-free land lease for industrial park developers.

PPPs run under Proclamation No. 1076/2018, with a PPP Board chaired by the Ministry of Finance that approves pipeline projects, tenders and awards, and a PPP Directorate General acting as its secretariat.

risks.detail: Heavy reliance on foreign-sourced construction inputs creates supply chain vulnerabilities; the domestic construction industry grew only 5.4 percent against a 17 percent Ten-Year Plan target, and local firms' average time overrun is double that of foreign firms.
Intermittent instability in certain regions continues to disrupt project execution, and the ministry rates political and governance risk as Substantial.

The National Bank maintained a cap on private credit growth at 24 percent a year, while 20 of 28 banks exceeded their annual growth caps by March 2026, which can constrain financing for developers and buyers.
Housing-related inflation is high: inflation for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels rose to 28.3 percent in 2023/24 from 23.9 percent the year before.
